title: PhD in the Netherlands Without IELTS 2027: How the Employee Model Skips the Certificate
seoTitle: PhD Netherlands Without IELTS 2027: Employee Model Explained
seoDescription: Dutch PhDs are jobs: €2,900-3,700/month, no tuition, and English assessed in the interview — not by IELTS. Where the certificate is and is not required in 2027.
intro: In the Netherlands a PhD is an employment contract — and interviews, not IELTS, decide language. Where the certificate is genuinely optional in 2027.
description: How the Dutch employed-PhD model works without IELTS: salaries, contracts, English assessment and application strategy.
author: NextApply Team
excerpt: Dutch PhDs are jobs — interviews, not IELTS, decide language. Where the certificate is genuinely optional in 2027.
content:
The Netherlands runs the cleanest "no IELTS" PhD system in Europe, for a structural reason: a Dutch PhD is a job, not a study programme. You are hired as an employee with a four-year contract, a salary under the university collective agreement, pension contributions and paid holidays — and employers assess English the way employers everywhere do, in the interview. For applicants with an English-medium degree and good spoken English, that makes the certificate genuinely optional at a large share of Dutch universities.

Why Dutch universities often skip the certificate

Dutch graduate schools distinguish between the language of the degree programme (where proof is standard) and the language of the workplace (where it rarely is). For employed PhD vacancies — the majority of Dutch doctoral positions — our verification pass across live listings found universities that state explicitly that no English certificate is required: Twente’s graduate school, for example, waives tests when your previous education was in English, and Radboud and Wageningen hire through interviews in English with no test mentioned at all. Vacancy ads typically say "excellent English skills" without naming IELTS — the assessment happens across a 40-minute conversation, your writing sample and your references.

Where a certificate does appear, it is usually attached to scholarship-based admissions (fees-paying doctoral tracks) or programmes with external accreditation — IELTS 6.5-7.0 or TOEFL 90-100 equivalents. The rule of thumb: employed vacancy, interview decides; scholarship track, check the small print.

What the job actually pays

Dutch PhD salaries are collective-agreement business. Under the universities’ CAO, a doctoral candidate starts at about €2,900 gross per month and climbs to roughly €3,700 by year four — and the July 2026 agreement added a further 3.1 per cent plus €50 a month, pushing those numbers up again. There is no tuition to pay: employment replaces the fee model entirely. Our salary and contract guide breaks down the scale, holiday allowance and the year-by-year pay curve.

Who this suits — and who needs a plan B

  • Strong fit: applicants with an English-taught master’s, a focused research interest and interview confidence. Your master’s transcript in English does the documentary work; the interview does the rest.
  • Plan B needed: applicants whose English evidence is thin on paper — a certificate strengthens scholarship-track applications even when vacancies do not ask for it.
  • German-speaking routes: not relevant here — Dutch academia runs on English; the language you actually need for daily life is Dutch, and universities offer free courses to employees.

The application that converts

Dutch vacancies are advertised like jobs, with closing dates and formal portals — which means the CV, motivation letter and (increasingly) a short research pitch matter more than supervisor emails. Read the vacancy the way our advertisement guide teaches, tailor the letter to the project’s listed tasks, and apply within the first half of the window; many committees start screening early. When English evidence is mentioned only as "excellent command", attach your MOI letter proactively — it answers the question before anyone asks.

Reading the vacancy landscape

Almost every Dutch doctoral vacancy lives on AcademicTransfer, the national board that aggregates positions from all universities and medical centres. Three filters do most of the work: employment type (choose "PhD position" over "scholarship" — the employee track pays properly), discipline, and institution. Listings follow a fixed format — the project description, your tasks, requirements, and the employment conditions block quoting the CAO scale — so comparisons are unusually easy. Application portals typically ask for CV, motivation letter, transcripts and references in one pass; committees score against the listed requirements, so mirror their wording.

Two contract shapes exist. The standard four-year employment contract (the one this article describes) dominates. A minority of positions run as bursary-style places with a stipend rather than salary — legal for a narrow set of cases and worth reading carefully, because stipends carry no pension and weaker visa standing. When the vacancy says "36 hours a week" with a salary range, it is employment; when it quotes a flat monthly amount with no CAO reference, ask before accepting.

Practical notes for moving

Housing is the real bottleneck in the Netherlands, not paperwork — university housing for international staff is scarce and waitlisted, so start searching at offer stage. Family matters are straightforward: PhD employees can bring partners, who receive full work rights.
